utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There are no preliminaries. Therefore, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Lukic -- is the witness on its way? Mr. Lukic, yesterday Mr. Gengo marked again D476 which was then admitted anew with a better, visible marking. Now, the same problems do exist in relation to D474 and D475. Whether it will be you or whether it would be Mr. Weber who does this exercise is relatively -- I don't mind who of the two takes that action. But we'd like to have marked maps clearly marked and so perhaps it should be done again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it is okay, I will leave it to Mr. Lukic. I would have no objection to him approaching that in re-examination, just because I'm not fully familiar with the witness's previous markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gengo. Before you -- we continue, I'd like to remind you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Weber will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. Gengo.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yesterday we left off discussing your responsibilities between February 1995 and the end of the war with respect to logistics. I'd like to pick up on that topic at the beginning of today. During your interview that you had with members of the Karadzic Prosecution team on 16 of October 2012, this reference is at page 6 of that transcript, you were asked: "Were you often involved in getting munitions from the VJ for the VRS? " Your answer was: "As necessary, as they would send me, then I would go." Next question was: "During what period did you perform that function? Your answer: "As I stated, since 1995, since February 1995, March, February, March, maybe March 1995 till the end of the war." Do you stand by this evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P893.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, today, I'm just going to go through one document with you and ask you to assist us with the procedure that was involved with this. Sir, can you see the document on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 10 July 1995 request from SRK commander General Dragomir Milosevic for weapons and ammunition. I would like to direct your attention first to the initials that appear towards the bottom of the page on the left-hand side across from the -- to the left of the signature. There, the initials, SM --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The initials SM. Is it correct that these initials are those of Milivoj Solar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What are -- what is the significance of the -- these initials on this document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milivoj Solar was the chief of technical services in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and this was a technical matter. That's why he drafted this letter and any letter of this kind and signed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that once Mr. Solar would draft these documents, it would then be presented to Dragomir Milosevic for his approval and signature?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, if we could please go up to the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This request is addressed to the VRS Main Staff. Is it correct that the SRK then directed its request for munitions --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please wait for me to finish my question. Is it correct that the SRK directed its requests for munitions to the Main Staff for its approval?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. They couldn't do anything without the Main Staff. Things had to go along the line of command, and that's how they were approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The last full sentence on this document, which, I believe, is down in the English or possibly on the next page. I believe it's actually on the next page states: "Our authorised representative, Slavko Gengo, will collect the requested approval and personally deliver it to the VJ for further action." Excuse me: "... deliver it to the responsible organs in the VJ for further action." Is it correct that General Mladic or one of his subordinates in the logistics sector of the Main Staff, such as General Djukic, would approve the request and then you would take it to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how things were done. Because of their urgency, those documents had to be urgently approved and then I had to go to Yugoslavia with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who did you take it to in the VJ, in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where was that located? In Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And you would personally report to the General Staff of the Yugoslav army, the VJ; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to the General Staff but to the logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's all I have for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Gengo, for the rest of today, I'm just going to hit on a couple of matters that were loose ends from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the Prosecution could please have P6537.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, sir, I'm going to be directing to sub-point 3 when this comes up. I -- I'm returning to the topic of the documents that followed the Markale shelling, and the -- the possible references in them. This document was admitted yesterday but I didn't put any questions to you. At this time I'd like to read you -- direct you to a specific part of this document, and read to you your previous question and answer that was asked to you during the Karadzic proceedings. In the Karadzic case, this is at transcript page 29816, after you'd been asked some questions, you were asked the following: "Again, there's no reference to a visit of a Joint Commission; although, it does at paragraph 3 refer to a meeting on events in Sarajevo which was held in the corps command attended by President Karadzic, General Gvero, UNPROFOR, and UN representatives." Your answer was: "Yes, I can see that." The next question was: "So you agree that there's no reference in this document anywhere to this visit of the Joint Commission that you've given evidence about?" Your answer was: "Yes." Do you stand by that evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I would like to say that I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir -- sir, you've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the witness wants to add something which is directly related to the question, you have an opportunity to do so. If it's not related to the question, you are invited not to say anything. So please make up your mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is related to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said "directly related." If it is, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the commission that visited us, that Gvero knew about that, and he was informed about the entire event by the commission that had visited us. That's why there's no reference to that commission in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that this is the very first between your previous statements, your previous testimony, every occasion that you've ever discussed this commission, that you've mentioned that the -- the possibility of General Gvero knowing about the commission?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure he knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, sir. Is this the first time that you've every mentioned the possibility of General Gvero knowing about this commission?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never mentioned that before. I'm mentioning it here. But, in conversations, I said that that was the case --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The last matter -- and, Your Honours, before going back into that, I apologise for the confusion yesterday. The incorrect statement was uploaded when I called this out. It was the Mladic statement and that's my fault. I'm going go back into that now and -- and explore his earlier Karadzic statement now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct you still have in front of you your Mladic statement that has the big letter M in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 7 of 65 ter 30664.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you recall, I had referred you to paragraph 31 of your current Mladic statement, and now I'm going to ask you a question about a paragraph from your earlier Karadzic statement. Your Karadzic statement -- excuse me, strike that. Your Mladic statement is almost verbatim from your Karadzic statement with a couple of additional paragraphs. What I'm going to be focussing on is the one sentence that was not included in your Mladic statement from your Karadzic statement. I'd like to direct your attention to paragraph 27 of your Karadzic statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, what we see on the screen now, is that the Mladic statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- or the Karadzic statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. It is the Karadzic statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So, sir, just so there is no confusion, what have you in front of you on the desk is your Mladic statement and what appears on the screen before you is the Karadzic statement, which I'm going to read to you since there's no translation for it. In paragraph 27 of the Karadzic statement, it starts the same. It says: "Occasionally groups of snipers armed with sniper rifles and passive scopes, sniper fire at night would come to the zone of responsibility of the unit opposed of [sic] us. They would fire against our positions and leave the area." Now in paragraph 27 of your Karadzic statement there 's an additional sentence. It states: "The Muslim local population regularly protested against their stays because they knew that the Serbian side's response would follow." Is this -- do you stand by this additional sentence, first of all?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you explain to us the reason that you did not include this sentence in your current Mladic statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did mention that, but this is a shortened version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: To understand correctly, when you say you did mention that, on the four occasions that you met with the Mladic Defence, you mentioned this to them.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned all of that. Since the indictments for General Mladic and President Karadzic are identical, my statements were also identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And is it then your evidence that -- well, did the Mladic Defence, then, draft your statement in this case based on what you said?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I met with them, I said what I had to say. They drafted my statement and sent it to me. They may have omitted things when they were typing up my statement, but that's up to them. All I'm saying is that my statement was identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And when you reviewed your statement, did you not ask for this additional sentence to be included in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. Their version was shortened so I thought, if that was the case, I don't see a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you responded to these snipers who would fire and leave the area with mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the area from which they fired. If they fired from a forest that allowed us to open only mortar fire, we did that. If we could use the 64-millimetre cannon, we used that. Or 20-millimetre or 12-millimetre. It all depended on the position from which the sniper shooter had opened fire and it all depended on our decision as to what would be the best weapon to neutralise that target.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Milomir Savcic interviewed you in the Karadzic case and took your Karadzic statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Before I invite the Defence to put further questions to you, it's -- it's a bit -- I'm a bit puzzled in the way in which these statements were created. If they are in many respects verbatim the same, and, of course, the Chamber doesn't have the other ones but that's what I understand, and I'm looking both to you, Mr. Weber, and to you, Mr. Lukic, that they are to a large extent literally and verbatim the same. Now, you've given that statement in the Karadzic case. It was put on paper. Now, if you are newly interviewed for days and days, then I would be a bit surprised that the text that results from those interviews is exactly the same in many respects as the previous one. Did they write that down when you were interviewed by the Mladic Defence, or did they just have the statement before them and went through it together with you? Could you explain to me how this was done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They made notes. They did make notes. I answered their questions. I remember my answers, the previous ones and the ones that I gave them. I may have changed things slightly, but even ten years after today, my answers would still be the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But did they have that old statement before them or was your memory such that you could verbatim repeat your answers as they appear in the Karadzic statement? These are two questions. The first is whether they had that statement before them when they interviewed you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't. They may have had it among their other paper, but they did not have it on them, there and then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you saw was them making notes, not visibly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- looking at or explicitly referring to your Karadzic statement. And then, on the basis of that, an almost verbatim statement was produced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see my previous statement in the Karadzic case with them, when I saw them. In any case, they just put questions to me in a certain order, in particular, since the indictments seemed to be nearly identical. And I simply provided my answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear to me. Mr. Mladic, there's no problem in taking your jacket off out of the courtroom and so not disturbing the -- please be seated. I have a question for you in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I put another question to you, I'd first give an opportunity to Judge Fluegge to ask you any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We still have the statement used in the Karadzic case on the screen. If I compare this page with the paragraphs 24 to 28, I see another difference when I read the statement given in the Mladic case. Paragraph 29 of the Mladic case starts with: "The deficit of professional commanding officers ..." It's the same as paragraph 26 in the Karadzic statement. What -- the next paragraph which follows in the Mladic statement is paragraph 30 and it reads at the beginning: "I was commander of the battalion for 16 months." This is not included in the Karadzic statement. Do you have any explanation why such an additional paragraph appears in the Mladic statement, in comparison to the Karadzic statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They probably asked me. I provided answers, and they noted them down in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one follow-up question in this respect as well. They made notes during the interviews. They prepared a statement. Now, how and when did you receive that written statement which you finally signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I received it in Sarajevo, in Lukavica. I don't remember the date exactly that -- that their team came and I signed it there and then in their office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there any further discussion about the statement? Did you have any -- was it sent to you by mail before you were invited to sign it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They personally brought it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They brought it to their office where you looked at it. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have a few more questions on a totally different subject. If I did understand your testimony well, you said that your troops at Spicaste Stijena were not closer than 10 metres to the edge and that they were subject to grenades being thrown at them and that they were fired at. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Our defence at Spicaste Stijena was behind the ridge, the edge of the rock. Some 10 metres away is where my positions were. The Muslim forces, when they attacked, they -- they would climb up the hill, reach the edge, and used hand-held rocket-launchers, Zoljas and Osas to engage us. But first they would approach us, they would come close. They launched such attacks in order to take our positions. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now just for me to imagine, I have a -- a cliff, more or less, because that's what Spicaste Stijena is, if I understand it well, and they are at 10 metres -- well, let's say, the distance between me and that door, now they climb up there. You are here in your positions. They take -- they take hand-held rocket-launchers, start shooting at you. And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they would fire at the trenches. We threw hand grenades. So we exclusively used hand grenades, and we also called for mortar support to fire at the foot of Spicaste Stijena so that they wouldn't be able to spread into a skirmish line to take Spicaste Stijena. So we would actually engage their troops on the other side of the ridge, of the edge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what you described seems to be an attack aiming at taking over control of the ridge of the cliff which is there. How often did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It happened on several occasions and on one such occasion they even seized three of our trenches. There were killed soldiers on our side, but the next night we managed to regain those trenches. On one occasion they also managed to take Mala Tvrdjava at Spicaste Stijena, because it was the shortest route for the Muslim troops to link up with their 3rd Corps in the sector of Ilijas --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the last location the witness mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last location you mentioned. What the interpreters heard was that you said: "... shortest route for the Muslim troops to link up with their 3rd Corps in the sector of Ilijas ..." And what did you say after "sector of Ilijas"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nabozic, it's a plateau where we had positions. They also attacked us there constantly from the direction of the 3rd Corps. They were trying to link up the 1st and the 3rd Corps so as to encircle a part of Sarajevo such as Ilidza, Hadzici, Ilijas, and Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just invited you to again mention the location you mentioned before. Now you said this happened several --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ravni Nabozic, that is the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said this happened on several occasions. Five times, eight times, three times, that such an attack, an attempt to take over happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They managed to take it twice. They did try several other times but failed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Several other times is another three times, five times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three or four times. They attacked with less intensity, thus failing to take those positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, that is then a couple of days during the whole of the conflict where these attempts were made. On the days where there were no such combat operations in order to gain or to regain, you always -- your men always stayed away 10 metres from the ridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You never came any closer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At Spicaste Stijena.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not. We couldn't because we were exposed to sniper fire on both our flanks. They fired at us, the Muslim forces, that is, and they managed to come quite close because it was a forested area. Any coming out on the ridge was very dangerous because one could be killed. Only when there was fog or really bad weather we could do so, but then we couldn't see anything anyway. We were exposed to so much enemy fire that we simply could not come out onto the ridge or do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You also told us that one of your soldiers was hit when picking cherries. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was 100 metres behind the line, behind the trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So now I do understand that you're so cautious not to come any closer to the ridge but at the same time someone in the middle of a armed conflict goes cherry picking and is shot at, exposes himself to fire from the other side. I'm trying to imagine that you hardly dare to move for 10 metres and that, at the same time, someone walks around and is hit at close to that same area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was 100 metres behind the lines, where there were houses already. The settlement. He was in a courtyard. People lived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What then did your troops do there, sitting there -- I'm talking about the days when there was no combat operation as described, which may have happened five or seven or eight times. What they were doing there? Just waiting, doing nothing? Did they fire at anything or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They stood guard in shifts, guarding the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And nothing happens. There was never any fire exchanged which was not related to such gaining or regaining territory operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If their snipers opened fire, of course, there would be an exchange. We tried to neutralise them. When this lad was killed, of course, we had to return fire in order to neutralize that position and respond to fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you tell me where, and we're talking about that incident, where that sniper position on the opposite side was located. Was it down the ridge or ... where was it from where --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, to the right. To the right of my positions. Towards the repeater station, if you remember the picture from yesterday, the panoramic photograph. So to the right from Spicaste Stijena towards the repeater station, that is where they had snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they have snipers any further down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They couldn't go down the cliff. They could only go to the left or to the right of Spicaste Stijena. There would be no point at targeting the cliff itself. They had snipers on the left and on the right of the cliff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber has received evidence about civilians being hit at Sedrenik. In your statement, paragraph 39, you say it was impossible to fire on Sedrenik with infantry weapons for two reasons. And I'll focus now on the first one. Firstly, because of the distance. Was the distance to Sedrenik an obstacle to fire at anyone located in Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We discussed sniping. We didn't discuss any kind of fire. We talked about snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. My question is: Was the distance -- by the way, the statement says "infantry weapons." I read it to you literally. "There were no trained snipers in my battalion. It was impossible to fire on Sedrenik with infantry weapons for two reasons ..." So that combines snipers and infantry weapons, although, the distance, the obstacle of the distance is not specifically related to sniping but is put in the context of the use of infantry weapons. Now, could you tell me, snipers or other infantry weapons, was the distance such that you could not hit with an infantry weapon from Spicaste Stijena someone who was located in Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our snipers could engage at 800 metres maximum, in order to hit the target. Anything beyond that did not guarantee any kind of hit. It was impossible to reach the target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you say that all of Sedrenik is at a distance of more than 800 metres from Spicaste Stijena? And for the record, I said: "... all of Sedrenik is at a distance of more than 800 metres from Spicaste Stijena."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not along the entire edge. The intersection at Sedrenik is 1350 metres away from Spicaste Stijena as I specified in the statement. The intersection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the reason why I'm asking you whether all of Sedrenik and not just an intersection, which I do not know which one you're referring to. I do not know whether you measured the distance accurately or not. But my question is whether all of Sedrenik is at a distance of more than 800 metres from Spicaste Stijena.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not all of it. In certain parts, they were closer, but there was no one in the houses in those areas. In any case, the empty houses were mostly Serbian houses and the people had moved out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there were no houses where people were living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were some, but I don't know how many exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you said a second ago, "there was no one in the houses in those areas," is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian houses, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read the whole of the answer. "In certain parts, they were closer, but there was no one in the houses in those areas. In any case, the empty houses were mostly Serbian houses and the people had moved out." This is -- the beginning of the answer is quite clear. All houses were empty. And then it's further specified in a rather confusing way. Why did you say that these houses were empty? What was the relevance of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We ask for audio to be checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- of course, if there's any problem there then, as always, Mr. Lukic, you know that I'm, myself, very much interested in detecting if there's any translation issue. Now why did you consider it relevant that those houses were empty? Why did you mention that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serb inhabitants had moved out. I said that the Serbian homes were empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I heard what you said. But why did you refer to the houses being empty? I didn't ask for it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the point of the question? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll tell you what the point of the question is. I wondered whether you were explaining to me why it would be of no use anyhow to fire at those houses if there's no one there. I wondered what came to your mind that you considered it important to tell us that the houses were empty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I thought -- I had in mind the Serbian people who had moved from there. I didn't have in mind the Muslim population. This is what it concerned. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you about the distance between Spicaste Stijena and houses -- Sedrenik. I asked Sedrenik. I did not even mention houses but ... And then you said the houses were empty anyhow. What's the relevance of that? Was that that there was no need to fire at them or what -- what else could be the relevance of bringing this to our attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We never opened fire at civilians. I don't know why you're asking me this. To my mind, there's no point to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Whether there's a point to the question is for me to decide. I didn't --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The witness concluded his answer by saying: In my mind, it is a provocative question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not provoking you; I'm examining you. We started with your answer that it was too far anyhow to fire at Sedrenik with infantry weapons. I then asked you, after you had explained that the range was not beyond 800 metres, whether all of Sedrenik was away from more than 800 metres. And then you start explaining that the houses in Sedrenik were empty, and I'm asking myself: What triggered you to bring to my attention that the houses in Sedrenik were empty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the Serbian population had moved out. The Serbian homes were along the edge. It didn't concern anything else. That was my understanding. I don't know what yours is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what's the relevance of Serbian houses being empty? What's the relevance of that for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was important because they could no longer live there. They had to retreat to their territory, and that is the part they were defending. They were at positions behind their houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I move on. Do you agree with me that the distance in itself was not an obstacle to engage parts of Sedrenik with infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was no obstacle but one could not engage precisely. It is impossible to be precise beyond 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think you agreed with me that the distance was, for parts of Sedrenik, less than 800 metres. So you could be precise in targeting anything that was closer than 800 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to target just anything, only military targets. Civilians were not targeted. You cannot put that under the same topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't talk about civilians. My question was whether you could target at less than 800 metres with precision with infantry weapons. I wasn't saying whether you were targeting a -- a house, a cow, a military sniper nest. I didn't say anything. Less than 800 metres, that's the only thing I said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll repeat. I wasn't referring to targeting civilians. I was just asking about hitting a target at a distance less than 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One can engage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any Muslims still living in parts of Sedrenik less than 800 metres from Spicaste Stijena?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There probably were, but I did not check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you any knowledge about shields of whatever sort being erected in Sedrenik with the obvious purpose of protecting yourself against fire coming from Spicaste Stijena? Shields from whatever material made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall that. I don't remember any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber received evidence that that was how people locally protected themselves against incoming fire. And now I'm talking about civilians. Does this ring any bell to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said that we received evidence that people locally protected themselves against being fired at, and I'm talking about civilians. Any knowledge about such measures taken by the local population that remained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, possibly, in terms of exchange of gun-fire, of course, there had to be protection so that a stray bullet in combat would not threaten somebody's life. They were probably trying to protect their own lives because they were close to the separation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 700 metres away, sometimes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that happened too because the lines were nearby. There was 100 metres between my positions and the positions of the Army of the Federation. In exchanging gun-fire, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about civilians at a distance of approximately 8 -- 700 metres from your lines. I'm not talking about others. I was talking about civilians, as I explained clearly to you, erecting shields to protect themselves. That's something different from what you describe; that is, the combatants protecting themselves. Distance of 700 metres. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I explained it nicely. When there's an exchange of gun-fire, not only sniper fire, machine-gun fire and any other kind of fire, and shooting from hunting guns, I'm talking about exchange of gun-fire. The population, nobody could stop a bullet, so when there was exchange of gun-fire, people could be hit if they did not protect themselves and if they went out of their houses, especially the side where the fire is coming from. I mean, if a machine-gun is firing, you cannot -- well, you know what it's like. It's a front line. There's an exchange of gun-fire. People had to protect their homes and the paths that they had to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that you would do that only if it was a frequent occurrence that bullets would come in? I mean, for a stray bullet once a week or once a month, it would make no sense to ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Opening fire was not only once, whatever. A cease-fire would go on for a few days and then again, and it changed all the time. It wasn't really that way. There was fighting and exchanges of gun-fire all the time. So they could not put up protection every day and then take it down and then put it up again. Once protection was there, it was supposed to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I understood your testimony to be that there was no visibility. You could not even look down into the valley. And it was only to the left and to the right that you were firing at their sniper positions, not down into the valley. You didn't even have a view on that, you told us, because you were 10 metres away from the ridge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, please, the front is wider. We were just talking about Spicaste Stijena. There's the right side and the left side. They did not attack only there. They attacked along the entire front line. But the main point was to get to Spicaste Stijena. That was easier to access. When there is an attack, then it's a frontal attack. It not against one point only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they came right in front of Spicaste Stijena and you were firing in that direction as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, please. When there's an attack, the attack takes place along the entire front line. Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- we -- Mr. -- witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we discussed the attacks, over a long period of time, perhaps five, six, or seven days. I'm talking about the days when there was no attack. I'm talking about those days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no firing then. There was no shooting then. There was no need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the Chamber received evidence that people were hit at the -- those days as well. And that they protected themselves against that kind of fire. If you can't tell us anything about it or if you do not have another explanation as to the one you gave us, we'll leave it to that. But I would want to give you an opportunity to further explain to us that situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, give me a document. I can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm telling you what we received as evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it doesn't have to be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will further assess whether the evidence is accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are a little bit beyond the time where we usually take a break, but Judge Fluegge has one further short question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Some minutes ago you said: "People had to protect their homes and the paths they were -- that they had to take." What kind of protection did you see at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they protected it either with sandbags or fences. I mean -- I mean, logs, wood. I cannot say. Different things. Whatever they had. They tried to make do, the people who stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means you were aware of such shields to protect the local population; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I saw that they had something. I mean, that really could be seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and -- could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you give us an indication as to how much time you would need for the re-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With maps that he has to mark, probably a bit more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could start already with preparing the maps, to ask Madam Registrar to be on standby to show to the witness what was it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. We need first D474.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will need top part of the city. North-east, actually. If we can enlarge that part. Actually, am I given the right to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- continue or you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First we'd like to tell the witness that you'll now be further examined by Mr. Lukic, Mr. Gengo, and one of the things he will start with is to seek the markings on the maps you made in another case, to make it better visible. So that's a purely technical matter with which he'll start.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, once again.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you walked in today, we were instructed by the Court to mark the maps again because, indeed, it is barely legible in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in a bit more? Could you please go right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could the usher already assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] I think if we save, Your Honours, if we save this, it's already marked and it's better visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we all agree on where the line starts. I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the line a bit better. Perhaps the witness could -- you marked on this map, Witness, the battalion's line of defence. Could you perhaps do that again so that it's better visible for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the map now marked again by the witness would receive number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D479, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Could we then have D475, I take it, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. So D475, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually maps take slightly longer to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you give instructions as to focus on what part of this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, the same part probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. We can stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gengo, on this map as well, you marked the positions of the artillery pieces that belonged to your unit. Could you please try to find this again on the map and then could you make the lines thicker?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can barely see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any position further down? I can't see that. But if you take the three now blue dots, if you -- that's one I thought I -- the Chamber had detected as well. It's these four positions, Witness, which you marked, or did we forget one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D475 as marked by the witness receives number D480, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D480 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gengo, I will start from the end; that is to say, I will start with today. I don't know how clear it's been. You spoke about a few attacks of Muslim forces when they took over your positions and a few attacks when they did not manage to do that. As for such attacks, would you characterise them as offensives by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably, probably these were their offensives, because they had their objective to link up with the other forces. That is what they had intended all along. Now, it is well known what their ultimate objective was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from these offensives, and Judge Orie asked you about this as well, tell us, was fire opened from their positions against your positions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, all the time there were provocations, especially when teams of snipers came, probably from other units. Snipers that were trained and they came with special instruments, and they opened fire against my positions day and night.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about your snipers? Could they fire during the night?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not have the right instruments for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an example of when they fired during the night?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the exact day -- date, I mean, but I know that on that day, in the area of Hresa, they killed three people, Mihajlo Jovicic, Karisik Nedjo, and Cicko [phoen] Maletic. All three were hit in the head during the night, pitch-dark. This was special ammunition, special snipers, so the victims did not save -- did not stand a chance. There was no way of having their lives saved. They were hit in the head, in the region of the eye, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, at the time --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, go along -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your units, who had better weapons, the Serb side or the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as snipers are concerned, they had much better weapons and people who were much better trained because they were equipped probably by the international community and I don't know who else. They had equipment that was far more precise and stronger than ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let us leave sniper activity and offensives on the side. How often was fire opened at your positions at Spicaste Stijena from automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It couldn't have been automatic rifles. That was not possible. It was only snipers, from left and right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. You said to us that Muslim positions were about 100 metres away from you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These empty houses that had been abandoned by the Serbs in Sedrenik, how far away were they from your positions? Do you know now?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends. It depends. In the area of Faletici, they were nearby. That was right in front. And as for Spicaste Stijena, it was down there below the hill. I cannot say exactly. Say, 300, 400 metres away. From the top of Spicaste Stijena, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just to interrupt. I do not believe it's clear on the transcript what the location was that was just mentioned. I believe I heard it, but I didn't -- I don't want to repeat it right now. I'm referring to line 18 of page 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, usually if we find such a sign, it means that they'll work on it, and I think the witness -- at least it was -- I heard Faletici. But that's -- usually if there's such a sign, the transcript will be revised later. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Judge Orie asked whether you could precisely target targets that were 700 metres away from your positions, and the snipers, so -- please just wait for my question to finish. From your positions, from your trenches --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what area --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The other side of Spicaste Stijena.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you fire at targets that were 100 metres away on the other side because of the configuration of the ground, the terrain?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on the left-hand side Spicaste Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, the other side of Spicaste Stijena.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. Left side, right side, there were woods there. It was a forest. Who would you fire at? I could not see at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were asked about obstacles and protection of the population in terms of optical visibility. In Sedrenik, from Spicaste Stijena, could you see these protections, these shields? Not from Spicaste Stijena but, rather, from your positions.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From our trenches?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see such protective barriers around Serbian houses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From your trenches?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, in that context, could I ask the witness again to -- I'll read one of your previous answers about Serbian or other houses. I asked you: "Have you any knowledge about shields of whatever sort being erected in Sedrenik with the obvious purpose of protecting yourself against fire coming from Spicaste Stijena? Shields from whatever material made." Your answer was: "I don't recall that. I don't remember any." And now, since then, you started explaining first to Judge Fluegge and now again to Mr. Lukic, that you saw that at Serb houses. And I'm a bit puzzled by at one moment saying that, I don't recall that, I don't remember any, and then to give a -- an explanation, not once but now even for a second time, what you saw exactly. Could you clarify why, at one moment, you say you don't know, and another moment explain in detail what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the trenches on Spicaste Stijena you can't see anything, but from the left side you could see them. From other positions you could, but not from the trenches on Spicaste Stijena because you couldn't see anything from the trenches. Ten metres away from the trenches, the visibility stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was not from what you could see from your trenches in Spicaste Stijena. I asked you: "Have you any knowledge about shields of whatever sort being erected in Sedrenik ..." I didn't ask you whether you saw it from the trench, whether you heard about it, nothing of the kind. You said, no, "I don't recall that. I don't remember any." You didn't say, I couldn't see it from here, or I heard about it there, or I could see it. The two answers seem to be in strong contradiction, and I would like to give you an opportunity to explain why I hear answers which I feel are contradicting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about Spicaste Stijena from which you couldn't see anything. But you could see things from the side, and you could see it from the reports of my officers that were on the lines taken up by my unit, and I learned that from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May be things will become clearer if we, once again, look at P3, page 30. When the document appears on the screen, I will ask the usher to assist the witness in drawing Serb positions and other Serb positions, if they can be seen in the photo. That is, not only the positions of his units but of other units as well. I'm interested to find out whether Sedrenik could be observed from other positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so we have some clarity. If we could use two different colours if they're going to be different types of forces discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe -- yeah. Do we have a different colour than red?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have blue as you may have sen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but is it on? I don't know ... how do you turn it on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the usher assist the witness and you give instructions, Mr. Lukic, what colour to use --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it's the other colour already on, that's fine. We can proceed. I see they are nodding so it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see anything here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the picture is rather dark. That's a bit of a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tilt the screen a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe you will see better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I tried that with mine and it's not -- it's not very ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. But if I'm watching from above, it's much better. If you tilt -- can you tilt the screen? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's a slight difference. Perhaps you put the question first and before the witness starts marking we'll find out whether he will be able to make any such marking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gengo, look at the photo. Can you mark Serb positions? Not only yours, but others as well, on the other side. Were there any other Serb positions that you can see in this photo? I'm talking about the time when you were the commander of your unit.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only from Debelo Brdo where an MAP was deployed. If you had binoculars you could observe things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see those positions in the photo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. I did my best. But if you can't, you can't.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the image is too dark. I can't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Forget the photo in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday the Prosecutor -- the Prosecutor asked you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'm going to call up P4610 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here, we can see that UNPROFOR representatives detected fire, and it says here that 70 per cent of -- as you can see in the text, was on the separation line.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there's a reference to explosions. And further down, it says that there was a tense exchange of fire in Ilidza throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether UNPROFOR troops recorded 20-millimetre machine-gun shots and Bofors [Realtime transcript read in error "buffer"] shots as explosions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so, because every round from a 40-millimetre weapon is -- disperses and looks like an explosion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It's not calling for speculation. Although the answer seems to be -- to contain some speculation but not because the question is -- the question was whether he knew why this was recorded in the way as they did. If you know, tell us. But if you have just thoughts about it, then please tell us that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was: Do you know whether UNPROFOR troops recorded 20-millimetre machine-gun shots and Bofors, which is a 40-millimetre weapon, as explosions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you first take us exactly where we read that, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We should hear the audio. Now can I see that it's not -- I said Bofors; here it says "buffer" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where are we, in what paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's 36th page, 22nd line. It says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Recorded. But where do I find the recording exactly. Could you take me -- is that on the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, it's in the transcript. In the transcript, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said: "Do you know whether UNPROFOR troops recorded 20-millimetre machine-gun shots and buffer shots as explosions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but it wasn't "buffer shots," it's "Bofors." It's type of the gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay, that now is -- okay. So whether they did that. Do you know whether they recorded it as explosions? Did they or did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They could record shots from 40-millimetre Bofors, from 30-millimetre Praga, and from PATs, which were 20-millimetre calibre, because their rounds fragmented when they hit their targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. The first question was whether they did that, yes or no. That was the question, Mr. Lukic. Do you know whether they recorded 20-millimetre machine-gun shots and Bofors shots as explosions? Did they record them like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no 20-millimetre machine-gun. Only a cannon can have 20-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then, Mr. Lukic, then you have to reconsider your question because the witness says that you're asking for something that doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The PAT that you mentioned, or the anti-aircraft 20-millimetre gun, how many rounds can it fire in a minute?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: 600 rounds in a minute, in theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So its fire is a burst of fire, like a machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a burst of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about the Swedish gun, Bofors. Does it also have a burst of fire?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Individual fire not bursts of fire. It works on the principle of a pistol. That's how Bofors acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, since you are not sure whether they recorded those shots or not --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I thought maybe somebody from UNPROFOR put you in the picture.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't. If they recorded such fire, they could do it based on the explosions resulting from such fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up P542 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And both speakers are invited to make a pause between question and answer in the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document was issued on the 5th of February, 1994. We're talking about a document now. And this document refers to the fire which was opened on the day when the incident at Markale took place, the first incident in Markale.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The time of the document is one o'clock, 13 minutes and 34 seconds in the morning.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the second page. The date is still the same but the time is 09.19.51 a.m. This time precedes the time on which the incident at Markale is said to have happened; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Are you done with the document, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you have questions, you can take over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because we looked at -- this is now the second one you showed. And let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can go back to the first one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Perhaps give me ... I'm just trying to find the time which you referred to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's on the top right corner, first line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First line. I have on this -- the document which is now -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Could we now look back at the first page. Look ... I'm looking because there's also the 4th of February is mentioned there as well. I see both a reference to the 5th and to the 4th, in the evening, and I had no opportunity yet to read the content. Just trying to understand exactly the gist of what ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The reporting obviously was the latest time. But the events, you are right, are even from the 4th of February. Because the update to UNMO Sarajevo was on the 4th of February, 1994. It says on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. You would say both are proceeding the time of the -- of the shell that fell on the Markale, and apparently one is a report which was prepared at the night of the 4th and most likely then sent in the early morning hours of the 5th. Whereas the other is sent later that same morning but still well before midday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I -- I'm with you again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Weber was on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's okay. I see that the Chamber was able to work it through. I just would note that the reporting period which they relate to, I believe, is mentioned in the first line of the text, the time that it correlates to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It takes us sometimes a bit of time to get on top of matters. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic. And, again, the gist of it is to describe the situation as it was reported before what happened. Okay. Thanks. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gengo, with the exception of using snipers, did your unit use mortars to respond to sniper fire when such a mortar was in a forested area; and did you also use the 20- or 40-millimetre anti-aircraft guns to respond?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it "yes" to both questions or one of them? There are two questions there. Mortars and 20- or 40--millimetre guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Gengo already explained that if the sniper was in the woods, they would respond with the mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But you're asking two questions in one question, Mr. Lukic, and when the answer is just "yes," we don't know what it's a "yes" to. So if you can break your questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When there was a sniper in the woods, you usually tried to neutralise it by using mortars; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If sniper fire came from enemy lines, did you also use the anti-aircraft guns?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes they barricaded themselves in abandoned houses, and then we had to use anti-aircraft guns. It all depended on where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you only say that regarding Spicaste Stijena?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The entire area of responsibility of my battalion. The sector was some 9 kilometres long along the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's briefly look at P4476 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were asked about the document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the B/C/S, it is page 6, while in the English version page 8. It is the 26th of January, 1994. The SRK Command issued this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were asked about the ordered offensive operations.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to move to the next page in the English because we will be referring to item 5 that we can see at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S version. In particular, 5.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you explained the concept of offensive as opposed to improving one's tactical position.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In item 5, it reads: "Task of units." And in 5.1, we see the Smbr with --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does it stand for, the 1st Smbr?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Lukic wait with his questions and repeat his current question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're invited to make a pause between answer and question and could you please repeat your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's now go through it one by one. Let me read it out. 5.1: With main body of forces and with auxiliary forces, the 1st Smbr carries out a decisive defence for the following zone: To the right of Kneginjac, and Pavlovac, to the left, the right bank of the Zeljeznica river, with the following task: In active defence and cooperation with the 1st Rpbr and the 2nd Slpbr --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I, first of all, invite you to wait a while after Mr. Lukic has put his question to you and only then answer, and could you please repeat your last answer because it was lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You expanded the abbreviations.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What do you want me to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us again what does the 1st Rpbr stand for and the 2nd Slpbr?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade and the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade. These three brigades defended the area specified before in the order. And it says further down: Improve the tactical position held by the brigade -- brigade's forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what is the difference between offensive actions and improving position?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: An offensive action has its goal to take a location or a town. Defensive action means defending one's position. Improving one's tactical position means that, for example, the enemy dug some trenches close to our positions and we had to push them back to secure our positions and move them further away from the area we are defending.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are done with this part. I wanted to ask you briefly about something else. The Prosecutor obviously denies that an UNPROFOR commission and the VRS -- and a VRS commission ever attended this scene. That is to say that they never visited the positions of your units on the 6th of February, 1994. We saw an order -- actually, General Milovanovic's request that a mixed commission be formed, and you were also shown this document -- the next document which I want to have brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still have it under 65 ter number 10.000.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honours, this is Exhibit P6536.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Take a look at the underlined part.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And just before that, it says the following: "Since the UNPROFOR Command did not reply to the request of the VRS GS by 1800 hours as we had asked in the request, I telephoned the UNPROFOR command in Kiseljak and was then told by General Ramsey, the Chief of Staff of the UNPROFOR command for the former BH, that the Muslim side refused to take part in the establishment and work of a joint military expert commission."

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that there is a reference made in the document by the refusal of the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that UNPROFOR did not refuse to co-operate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the witness was invited to repeat the answer because, again and again, you are overlapping, and the answer was not recorded and not interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My mistake, actually. Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gengo --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I have a question for you, Mr. Gengo. Can you read the last paragraph of that document where it says: "The UNPROFOR command refuses to have the UNPROFOR Chief of Staff and the Chief of Staff of the so-called BH Army visit the crime scene together with the VRS Chief of Staff to ascertain the consequences and circumstances of this tragedy." So we're being told there that UNPROFOR refuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Look at the last --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it. But, please, in the upper part it says that it was upon the request of the Main Staff of the VRS command to UNPROFOR to have a joint commission established and so on and so forth. However, the Muslim army command refused. They refused UNPROFOR's request. It was rejected based on the Muslim side rejection. It wasn't that UNPROFOR rejected it first. We asked them both to participate but the Muslims refused. They were probably afraid of the truth because it would have been proven that Markale, as many other incidents in Sarajevo, were staged by them. Just like the case in Vase Miskina Street, and then Markale, then Tuzla, then Sefer Halilovic's apartment. It was done by the same group. They were probably waiting for something else. They staged it in order to prove their point and lay the blame on someone's -- someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Judge Moloto asked you to comment on the last sentence. Did you refer to that sentence as well, or did you only refer to the middle part? Apparently it -- we can read that the UNPROFOR Command refuses to have the UNPROFOR Chief of Staff and the Chief of Staff of the so-called BH Army visit the crime scene together with the VRS Chief of Staff to ascertain the consequences and circumstances of this tragedy.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO GENGO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Since the Muslim side refused and did not respond, then UNPROFOR decided to write what they did. In any case, it was the Muslim side that refused. They refused UNPROFOR's request to have a joint commission attend the scene. So they refused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, almost all of what is said now we heard that yesterday as well. It's -- it's slightly unclear to me what the issue is. It is clear from this document and the witness tells us, and I tend to agree with him, that it's clear from this document that the BiH Army refused to be part of such a commission. There is some dispute about whether the last lines express that UNPROFOR did not want to take part at all or that they did not want to take part at the level of Chief of Staff, that is, at least -- seems to be from the language not without ambiguity.
